explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. God says, “Mark out one road for the sword to come against Rabbah of the Ammonites, and another against Judah into fortified Jerusalem.” Rabbah is the Ammonites' city, sitting at the end of the second road. Two roads, one starting land, and a signpost at each branch. Ezekiel, the prophet, is basically drawing a map with a sword on it.

Nice try, friend, but Gaza isn't on this map. The text names only two destinations: Jerusalem and Rabbah of the Ammonites. Ezekiel only has two signposts to paint, and Gaza didn't make the cut. Rabbah is the other road.

Kir isn't on Ezekiel's signposts, baker. God says one road goes against Rabbah of the Ammonites and the other against Judah into fortified Jerusalem. That's the whole list. Two roads, two cities, and no third sign hiding in the dough.

Yes, an omen. Verse 21 says the king of Babylon stands at the fork “to seek an omen,” and then lists the arrows, the idols and the liver. That's a whole lot of effort just to pick a road. I make a batch of cookies without consulting any organs, friend.

Close in sound, but not what the text says. The king of Babylon stands at the junction “to seek an omen.” The arrows, the idols and the liver are all how he goes about it. A blessing isn't what he's after at that fork.

No ally shows up in this verse, baker. The king is standing at the fork in the road, and the text says he's there “to seek an omen.” He's trying to learn which road to take, so that's the word that fits the blank.
Not this time, friend. The text says, “In his right hand appears the portent for Jerusalem.” So the omen points him to Jerusalem, not to Rabbah. The Ammonites' road is the other one.

That's right, baker. Verse 22 says, “In his right hand appears the portent for Jerusalem.” The omen points to Jerusalem, and Rabbah isn't what shows up in his hand. Good catch on a sneaky little detail.
Right on, baker. The king is “to direct the battering rams against the gates.” The same verse lists a ramp and a siege wall too. It's a heavy list, so I'll just say the gates are the target.

Close to the neighborhood, but not in this verse. The text says he'll direct battering rams against the gates, and it also mentions a ramp and a siege wall. Siege towers aren't on the list. The gates are meeting battering rams.
Not this one, friend. The only arrows in these verses are the ones the king shakes to seek an omen. The thing he directs against the gates of Jerusalem is battering rams.

Yes, guilt. The omen “will draw attention to their guilt and take them captive.” To those who swore allegiance to the king, it will seem like a false omen. The text says it draws attention to their guilt anyway.

I see why you'd think it, since these folks have sworn allegiance. But the text says the omen will draw attention to their guilt. It seems false to them, yet it still takes them captive. Loyalty isn't the word in the verse.

Courage doesn't show up in this verse, baker. The omen “will draw attention to their guilt and take them captive.” That's what fills the blank. The ones who sworn allegiance to the king of Babylon just think the omen is false.

True, baker. The Lord GOD says the sins are revealed in all their deeds, and then, “you shall be taken in hand.” It's a sober verse, and I think it's one to read slowly. The text says it plainly, so we can too.

Actually it's true, friend. The Lord GOD says their sins are revealed in all their deeds, and then He says, “you shall be taken in hand.” That's right there in verse 24. It's a heavy one, so no wonder it's tempting to doubt it.

Yes, final. God says, “the day has come for your final punishment.” He's speaking to the profane and wicked prince of Israel, and the text calls the punishment final. It's a serious line, and the text doesn't soften it.
That's not the word, baker. God calls it “your final punishment.” Nothing in the verse says light. The prince of Israel is told the day has come.
Not delayed, friend. The verse says “the day has come for your final punishment.” God uses the word final, and the day has already arrived in His words. This is one of the heavy parts.

That's it, baker. God says, “Remove the turban, and take off the crown.” Those are the marks of a ruler, and God is telling them to come off. I wear a tall chef's hat, so I'd be nervous if someone told me to take mine off.
Not those two, friend. The Lord GOD says, “Remove the turban, and take off the crown.” No robe or ring in this order. Just the things worn on the head.
Swords are all over this passage, but not here. In verse 26, the Lord GOD says to remove the turban and take off the crown. The shield doesn't appear in these verses at all.
Right, baker. God says, “Exalt the lowly and bring low the exalted.” Two directions at once: one goes up and one goes down. And it comes right after “Things will not remain as they are.”

Wealthy isn't the word in this verse, friend. The Lord GOD says, “Exalt the lowly and bring low the exalted.” The text talks about the lowly and the exalted, not about money. Those are the two groups that trade places.

Careful, baker, this one flips things around. The text says to “bring low the exalted,” and the ones raised up are the lowly. Mighty isn't the word the verse uses. It's “Exalt the lowly and bring low the exalted.”

explanations.answer: The arrival of the One it belongs to
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. God says it “will not be restored until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs, to whom I have assigned the right of judgment.” The ruin waits for Him. I'll let that sit for a second.

explanations.answer: The end of seventy long years
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse, friend. God says the ruin “will not be restored until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs.” No number of years is named here. The condition is His arrival.

explanations.answer: The fall of the king of Babylon
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but the text doesn't say it. God says it “will not be restored until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs.” The king of Babylon isn't named as the condition. It's all about the One it belongs to.

Not quite, baker. God tells Ezekiel to prophesy about the Ammonites and their contempt, and the word is, “A sword! A sword is drawn for slaughter.” The omen pointing to Jerusalem doesn't put the Ammonites in the clear. They have their own message.

Yes, false. God tells Ezekiel to prophesy concerning the Ammonites and their contempt, saying, “A sword! A sword is drawn for slaughter, polished to consume, to flash like lightning.” Rabbah's road was on the map for a reason. This is a heavy word, and the text doesn't let them off.

Yes, baker. God says, “In the place where you were created, in the land of your origin, I will judge you.” The sword goes back in its sheath, and the judging happens right where they began. That's the text's own wording.
Egypt isn't named in this verse, friend. God says, “In the place where you were created, in the land of your origin, I will judge you.” The judgment is set in their own land of origin.
Edom isn't in this verse, baker. The text says, “In the place where you were created, in the land of your origin, I will judge you.” It's all about where they came from.
That's right, baker. The message ends, “You will not be remembered, for I, the LORD, have spoken.” I think this is a hard one to hear. It's a sober way to end, and it's what the text says.
That's not how this message ends, friend. God says, “You will not be remembered, for I, the LORD, have spoken.” Nothing in these last verses says restored. It's a heavy ending.
No ruling in this ending, baker. The last words are, “You will not be remembered, for I, the LORD, have spoken.” I think this part is heavy, and the text doesn't soften it.
